children.text: Built by the Franciscans from volcanic stone in

, this Baroque church faces Mayon Volcano from Santa Maria Hill. A National Cultural Treasure known for its Solomonic columns and octagonal bell tower, it is free to enter and pairs well with the Cagsawa Ruins for a half-day trip.

Daraga Church, formally Nuestra Señora de la Portería Parish (Our Lady of the Gate), stands on Santa Maria Hill overlooking the town of Daraga in Albay. It is one of the best-known Spanish colonial stone churches in Bicol, and thanks to its view over the town and plain to Mayon Volcano, almost every visitor to Legazpi stops here.
The church's history cannot be separated from Mayon. Fearing eruptions, the people of Cagsawa asked to move to safer ground, and the Spanish governor is said to have approved the request on
. Franciscan friars built the church from volcanic stone in
. When Mayon erupted catastrophically on
February 1, 1814
and buried the Cagsawa church, the survivors gathered here, and Daraga grew into the new center. The
Cagsawa Ruins
and this church are two scenes of the same story.

The style is described as Baroque mixed with Mexican Baroque and Renaissance Gothic, and architectural historians also call it Churrigueresque. The facade is laid with local volcanic stone and coated in lime for protection; over time this has weathered into a distinctive mottled texture of darkened stone and white plaster. The front has twisted columns set with medallions of the four Evangelists, and on the left rises an octagonal bell tower carved with the twelve apostles. The eastern and western facades, the bell tower and the baptistery were declared a National Cultural Treasure by the National Museum in
, and a historical marker from the National Historical Commission was unveiled on
October 16, 2008
It is still a working parish where Mass is held daily, so there is no admission fee, and
30 minutes–1 hour

is enough to see it. Still, climbing the steps on a clear morning and looking at the bell tower and Mayon together from the front plaza is a memory that lasts. It suits travelers interested in architecture and religious heritage, anyone who wants a photo with Mayon, and those planning a half-day Albay route together with the Cagsawa Ruins.

The four columns on the facade are spiral-twisted Solomonic columns, and each round medallion carries a stone carving of Matthew, Mark, Luke or John. The facade also lacks the vertical columns and horizontal cornices usually seen on Baroque churches. Step close and follow the grain of the carving slowly.

The tower on the left is octagonal; its four tiers narrow as they rise and end in a dome and cross. The six faces of the lower level carry the twelve apostles, and plants growing in the gaps show the passing of the centuries. Looking up from the foot of the steps gives the most dramatic angle.

blocks.title: Carvings above the door and the Latin inscription

children.text: The arch and wall above the main door are carved with Franciscan emblems, a papal coat of arms and the five wounds (stigmata) of St. Francis. Above the door is a Latin line meaning "the house of the Lord is well founded upon firm rock." The church was badly damaged in the
wartime bombing, but the stigmata carving is said to have survived.

From the plaza in front of the church and the upper steps, look north and a perfectly conical Mayon rises above the plain. Early morning, before clouds cover the summit, is best; in the afternoon you have to wait for a brief break in the clouds. A shot of the facade and the volcano together is the signature photo here.

blocks.title: The interior and the new altar

children.text: The interior was simplified between
and

to follow the guidelines of the Second Vatican Council. A gilded retablo has recently been installed behind the altar, adding warm light to the dim interior. During Mass, watch quietly from the back and get a feel for local faith.

On the wall below the bell tower is a historical marker placed by the National Historical Commission. It records the church's history and its value as heritage, and reading it before you walk around the facade makes everything easier to understand.

blocks.title: A loop with the Cagsawa Ruins

children.text: The Cagsawa Ruins, about
10 minutes
away by car, preserve the bell tower of the old church buried in the
eruption. See the tower and Mayon at Cagsawa in the morning, then the church built afterward at Daraga, and the history of Albay that links the two churches falls into place at once.

Philippine Airlines' PAL Express and Cebu Pacific fly daily from Manila Ninoy Aquino Airport (MNL) to Bicol International Airport (DRP), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
. One-way fares vary by season and are usually around
. The airport is in Daraga itself, about
6km
in a straight line and roughly
15–20 minutes
by car from the church.
When Mayon is active, ashfall can delay or cancel flights, so check airline notices before you leave.
Long-distance buses to Legazpi leave Manila several times a day from terminals such as Cubao. Companies including DLTB, ALPS, Cagsawa Bus and Bicol Isarog run the route, and the trip takes about
11 hours 30 minutes–12 hours 30 minutes
. Fares differ by class, from about
for a regular bus to about
for a reclining seat, though some companies quote lower prices.
Buses to Legazpi often pass through Daraga. Ask the driver to drop you at Daraga town hall or in front of Jollibee Daraga, and you can walk to the church steps.
The cheapest way is a jeepney from Legazpi marked "Daraga," about
and
20 minutes
. Get off at Daraga town hall or in front of Jollibee and climb the stone steps in the lane toward the church.
If the steps are a problem or you have luggage, a tricycle from Legazpi can take you close to the church; expect about
15–20 minutes
and
. Bargain, and agree on the fare before you get in. You can also ask about a half-day charter that covers the Cagsawa Ruins in one trip.
From central Legazpi the church is
15–20 minutes
by car. A rental car or a hotel-arranged taxi makes it easy to combine the Cagsawa Ruins and a trip toward Donsol.
The church is open all year, but the Mayon view that makes a trip here worthwhile depends on the weather. The drier months from
February
to
May
are best, and
March–April
often brings clear days with a crisp cone all the way to the summit. Even so, Bicol is rainy most of the year, and clouds and afternoon showers are common even in the dry season.
From
June
to
December
is the rainy and typhoon season, and between
September
and
December
in particular strong typhoons often cross Bicol and can halt flights and buses. During the day Mayon is clearest from sunrise until about
. Around sunset the clouds sometimes lift, letting you capture a red sky and the church silhouette together.

During Holy Week and Christmas, special Masses draw large crowds and the mood is solemn. If you visit then, plan your viewing around Mass times and dress with extra care. Mayon's alert level has also moved up and down in
, so check the latest notices from the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) before you go.

There is little lodging right next to the church, so most travelers stay in central Legazpi,
15–20 minutes
away by car. Mid-range hotels at about

a night are plentiful, and those with Mayon-view rooms or a rooftop cost more. If you are flying through Bicol International Airport, small hotels and homestays on the Daraga side are also convenient.

The food is mainly Bicolano. Be sure to try "Bicol Express," a spicy pork stew cooked in coconut milk and chili; "pinangat," taro leaves steamed with coconut milk and meat; and "sinantol," cooked in coconut milk. For dessert, pili-nut sweets, chili (sili) ice cream and Tiwi halo-halo are well known. Around the church hill and in central Daraga there are cafés and restaurants with open views toward Mayon, good for a rest after your visit.
If Mayon is your goal, arrive just after sunrise. After
the summit is often hidden in cloud.
The church is generally listed as open from
to
, though listings differ slightly. Check the Mass schedule on the board beside the Adoration Chapel.
Mass times differ by day and are mostly held early in the morning and in the evening. Avoid photographing the interior or making noise while Mass is under way.
Avoid sleeveless tops, short shorts and flip-flops; dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered.
The stone steps are long and steep, so wear non-slip shoes and take extra care after rain.
The bell tower and facade are cultural heritage. Do not climb on the carvings or touch, scrape or chip the stone.
To fit the facade and Mayon in one frame, shoot with a wide-angle lens from the lower part of the plaza. Early morning, when it is quiet, works best.
The Cagsawa Ruins are only about
10 minutes
away by car, so they combine well in the same half-day. Chartering a tricycle makes the transfers and waiting easier.
Mayon is an active volcano. Check PHIVOLCS alert levels and airline notices before you go, and follow evacuation and access instructions from local authorities.
After heavy rain, the risk of lahars (volcanic mudflows) on Mayon's slopes rises. Stay away from river channels and areas close to the volcano.
During Mass the church is a place of prayer for worshippers. Avoid flash photography, noise and walking toward the altar.
Be sure to settle the fee first with private guides and photographers who approach you at the church or on the steps. Watch your belongings and phone as well.
Agree on the fare and waiting time before you board a tricycle or chartered vehicle.
Mayon's alert level has moved between Level 2 and Level 3 in
. Daraga, where the church stands, lies outside the
6km
-radius Permanent Danger Zone, but ashfall or flight disruptions can occur, so check the latest notices before and during your trip.
